judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper proposes a universal quantitative measure for system organization based on the principle of least action. The author argues that organization is inversely proportional to the physical amount of action within a system. By modeling a closed, nondissipative system with a single free particle and one constraint, the study derives an expression where organization equals the reciprocal of the action integral. The derivation assumes constant mass and speed, isotropic media, and fixed endpoints. The model is applied to a specific case where two system states differ only in the trajectory length of the element due to constraint orientation. Results indicate that the state with the shorter trajectory (lower action) possesses twice the organization of the state with the longer trajectory. The author posits that this metric, grounded in fundamental physics, will empower natural and social sciences to quantify and compare organizational levels across diverse systems, facilitating the design of more perfect systems. The paper serves as Part 1 of a series, with future parts intended to extend the model to open systems and multiple elements.

Research Context
Measuring organization is a long-sought criterion for all sciences. Prior attempts relied on information theory or entropy concepts. The principle of least action has been applied to ecosystems. No universal method existed for measuring system organization.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how to quantify system organization. The hypothesis posits an inverse relationship between action and organization. The study predicts that lower action states are more organized. The model aims to provide a general calculation method.

Methodological Details
The study models a closed system in 2 dimensions. The system contains exactly one element and one constraint. The system boundaries are defined as a square. Elements are treated as free particles with zero potential energy. The Lagrangian is equated to kinetic energy only. The system assumes no energy dissipation occurs. Mass and speed of the element are held constant. Start and end points are fixed at opposite corners. The medium is assumed to be isotropic.

Procedures And Architectures
Organization is defined as the inverse of the sum of actions. The constant of proportionality is set to one for simplicity. Action integral is calculated using the Lagrangian over time. Time interval is substituted with trajectory length via velocity. Hamilton's Principle determines the actual trajectory. Organization for n=1 is the reciprocal of the action integral. Two states are compared based on trajectory lengths l1 and l2.

Key Results
State 2 has a shorter trajectory than State 1. State 2 is determined to be better organized than State 1. If trajectory l1 is twice l2, organization doubles. The ratio of organizations is the inverse ratio of lengths. There is a 50% difference between the two organizations. The second state is quantitatively twice as well organized.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The method relies on the principle of least action. Lower action corresponds to higher organization. The model facilitates comparison between different systems. This approach could empower natural and social sciences. The result enables the design of systems with higher perfection.

Contradictions And Limitations
The model is limited to closed systems. The system must be nondissipative. The model currently applies only to one element. The model currently applies only to one constraint. Extensions to open systems are planned for future parts.

Claims
Organization is inversely proportional to the physical amount of action in a system. The measure is inversely proportional to action. Organization equals the reciprocal of the action integral.  This allows quantifying organization in any system.
A state with half the action has double the organization. Half action yields double organization.  This enables direct comparison of organizational levels.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Robustness is tested via a limiting case of one element. Sensitivity to constraint orientation is analyzed.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 defines the boundaries and initial/final points. Fig. 2 illustrates two states with different trajectory lengths.

Three Takeaways
1. Organization is the reciprocal of the action integral. 2. Shorter trajectories indicate higher organization. 3. Future work will extend to open systems and n elements.
